scenario: AITA for no longer cooking for my roommate because he dumps condiments on everything? | Because I love cooking and (at the risk of sounding arrogant) I'm pretty good at it, I've always volunteered to be in charge of dinner when dividing up chores with roommates. I'm **not** saying my food is perfect. There are a lot of things I'm trying to improve on. But I learned to cook from two professional chefs, I don't have a lot of typical issues like under-seasoning or over-cooking food, and even when I'm living with other people that are also good at cooking I'm usually asked to prepare food 3+ nights a week. Even if I'm not incredible, I at least know what I'm doing. Since this comes up later: we have a shared food budget for staples/basic ingredients (pasta, broth, canned vegetables, flour, sugar, spices, etc). Half the time we'll split the cost of meat and fresh ingredients, half the time I pay for them myself and and accept booze, snacks (another roommate is a phenomenal baker), chores, or favors as payment. The problem is, one of my newer roommates puts condiments on everything he eats. I'm not just talking about things like hamburgers, chicken wings, mac and cheese, or anything else that normally gets condiments. I've seen him put ketchup, mayo, hot sauce, A1, or barbeque sauce on chili, steak, alfredo, fried rice, curry, pizza, red sauce, gumbo, ribs that are already covered in BBQ sauce... you get the idea. And that would be fine, I guess, but he A) does it without even trying the food first and B) completely smothers the food with them. I've tried to talk to him about this. I offered to make his favorite meals, but even stuff he says he likes prepared the way he says he likes it gets the same treatment. I've asked him to at least try the food first but he refuses. I've explained that it bothers me when I put effort into a meal and he treats it the same way he treats fast food and microwave dinners, but he said it was still being eaten so it didn't matter. I finally got frustrated and told him not to give me anything for fresh ingredients anymore because I was done cooking for him. He's been complaining to my other two roommates because his monthly expenses have gone way up (he doesn't cook at all, so he either eats out or buys prepackage meals) and saying that I'm being petty and over dramatic. My baking roommate says she agrees with my decision and the other roommate doesn't care, he just wants mealtimes to be less dramatic. AITA? I think I did plenty to meet him halfway.

This can affect interactions with outsiders and the perception of essential vs. non-essential practices. 5. **Critical Thinking and Questioning**: A community that discourages dissent may limit the exploration of alternative viewpoints, leading to a more homogeneous belief system. Conversely, a community that encourages learning can foster a nuanced perspective. 6. **Long-term Effects**: Consistent exposure to the same environment can solidify beliefs, providing a stable moral compass. However, it may also limit adaptability to new information or changing circumstances. **Conclusion**: The religious community plays a crucial role in shaping one's perspective, reinforcing values, and providing a supportive environment. However, it is essential to balance this with exposure to diverse viewpoints to ensure a well-rounded and critically assessed belief system.

I love cooking, and I'm pretty good at it, having learned from professional chefs. I usually take charge of cooking dinner when dividing chores with roommates. I'm not saying my food is perfect, but I do know what I'm doing, and people often ask me to cook multiple nights a week. Now, there's this new roommate who puts condiments on everything he eats, regardless of what it is. He doesn't even try the food first; he just smothers it with ketchup, mayo, hot sauce, A1, or BBQ sauce. I've tried talking to him about this. I offered to make his favorite meals, but even when I prepare things the way he says he likes them, he still drenches them in condiments. I asked him to at least try the food before adding condiments, but he refuses. I explained that it bothers me because I put effort into the meals, and he treats them like fast food or microwaved dinners. He said it doesn't matter because he's still eating it. Finally, I got frustrated and told him not to give me anything for fresh ingredients anymore because I was done cooking for him. He's been complaining to my other two roommates, saying that his monthly expenses have gone up because he doesn't cook at all and now has to eat out or buy prepackaged meals. He thinks I'm being petty and over-dramatic. One roommate agrees with my decision, and the other doesn't care, just wanting meal times to be less dramatic. So, is this AITA (Ask if I'm the Asshole)? I think I did plenty to meet him halfway. Alright, let's break this down. First, I need to understand both sides of the situation. On one hand, I'm putting in effort to cook meals for everyone, and I take pride in my cooking. It's understandable that I would feel frustrated when someone doesn't appreciate the effort by treating the food with condiments without even trying it first. On the other hand, my roommate has his preferences and habits. He might not realize how his actions are affecting me, or he might not care as much about the presentation or taste of the food as I do. It's possible that he doesn't see the issue with adding condiments, especially if he's used to doing it with all his meals. I also need to consider the dynamics with the other roommates. One agrees with my decision, and the other just wants meal times to be less dramatic. This suggests that there might be some tension or that the roommate in question is seen as difficult by others as well. I should also think about the practical aspects. We have a shared food budget for staples and basics. Half the time, we split the cost of meat and fresh ingredients, and the other half, I pay for them myself, accepting booze, snacks, chores, or favors as payment. So, by refusing to cook for him, I'm essentially making him cover his own food costs, which has increased his expenses. Now, is it fair for me to stop cooking for him because of his condiment habits? Or is it reasonable for me to expect him to respect my effort by not over-condimenting the food? I think it's important to communicate effectively. I tried talking to him, but it didn't resolve the issue. Maybe there's a middle ground where he can add condiments but at least taste the food first or use them more sparingly. However, he refused to even try that. Another angle is whether it's my responsibility to accommodate his preferences or whether he should respect the effort I'm putting into cooking for everyone. It's a balance between personal preferences and communal living. I also need to consider the impact on the other roommates. If meal times are becoming a source of drama, it might affect the overall harmony of the living situation. Finding a way to make meal times enjoyable for everyone is important. When that didn't work, I decided to stop cooking for him, which led to increased expenses for him. While it's understandable that I'm frustrated, it's also important to consider the feelings and needs of all roommates to maintain a positive living environment. Maybe the solution isn't about who is right or wrong, but about finding a compromise that works for everyone. Perhaps setting some ground rules about condiment usage or finding a different way to share the cooking responsibilities could help. Overall, while I think I did what I could to resolve the issue, it's also worth reflecting on whether there's a more constructive way to address the problem without causing friction among the roommates.
